title: About — Jon Martin
description: Jon Martin writes diagnoses of why systems and org structures keep breaking in founder-led professional services firms — and why the fixes didn't hold.
subhead: Most people who get called into a broken business are there to build something. That's the problem — the last three things you built are why you're calling.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: I'm Jon Martin, a revenue operations solutions architect. I spent 12 years building and running RevOps functions, and I founded two firms, scaled both, and sold both. Today I work in systems integration and subscription management, mostly for SaaS and professional services companies, and I treat the job as variety management, not tooling. What I write here are diagnoses of why systems and org structures keep breaking in founder-led professional services firms, and why the fixes didn't hold.

sections.heading: What I actually do
paragraphs: I work in revenue operations — systems integration and subscription management, mostly for SaaS and professional services companies. The job looks like tooling from the outside. It isn't. It's variety management: deciding what complexity a business should absorb, what it should refuse, and whether the answer is new tooling or a redrawn boundary.

That distinction is the whole reason this site exists. A company that can't quote consistently doesn't have a CPQ problem. A company whose reports nobody trusts doesn't have a dashboard problem. Those are symptoms of a structure that produces them reliably, and replacing the tool leaves the structure intact — which is why the new tool breaks in the same place the old one did.

sections.heading: Why a second opinion, and not a project
paragraphs: The highest-leverage move in operations is usually to move a team boundary, and that's almost never available to the person brought in to fix the process. I do a lot of my work as an external designer — hired to fix the system, not to redraw the org.

So the deliverable is a written diagnosis: here's what's actually breaking, here's the constraint you can't remove, here's what it costs you a year, and here's the best system available inside it. Naming a constraint you can't remove isn't failure. Pretending you can automate around it is.

sections.heading: Where the framework comes from
paragraphs: Four systems laws do most of the work: Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety, Conway's Law, Brooks's Law, and the Reverse Conway Maneuver — with Beer's Viable System Model behind them. I've written the whole thing up as a standing reference rather than re-explaining it per engagement, and separately as a plain-language series for anyone who'd rather start there.
